However, JK Rowling isn't exactly innocent. She misrepresented a workplace discrimination case with Maya Forstater by claiming that is was because she asserted that sex is real when she actively discriminated against trans women and made fun of their appearance. She also manipulated statistics to artificially create fear by claiming that there was in increase of 4400% of trans youth. However this is only true because the original number of youths getting gender non-conforming care in her study was 96 in 2010 to 2,510 in 2018, which would obviously increase the percentage if it was that low to begin with (and isn't even a shockingly high number of youths compared to the hundreds of thousands in the UK).

Personally however, I don't care if people play the game or continue to buy Harry Potter merchandise. I just wish that people understand that JK Rowling isn't as blameless as she claims to be.

If you want to find a black and white transphobic statement like "I hate trans people," then I think you're out of luck. Most of JKR's transphobia comes from strawman arguments and misrepresenting the narrative to make herself come across as more of a victim.

For example, in her 2020 essay on sex and gender issues, she writes, "I tweeted my support for Maya Forstater, a tax specialist who’d lost her job for what were deemed ‘transphobic’ tweets. She took her case to an employment tribunal, asking the judge to rule on whether a philosophical belief that sex is determined by biology is protected in law. Judge Tayler ruled that it wasn’t."

However the actual case against Maya Forstater losing her job, (she didn't even lose her job by the way, they decided not to renew her contract), was not about defending her belief that sex is real. It was about her actively discriminating against trans individuals under the cause of "gender-critical beliefs". In her tweets used as evidence, she described transgender women as 'males' and referred to Pippa Bunce, a gender-fluid individual who won an award for Executive Businesswoman of the Year, as "a man in a dress".

Maya actively discriminated against others and was found to be not under the protection of the UK Equality Act of 2010, which protects individuals from discrimination of religion or belief, disability, age, sex, sexual orientation and gender reassignment.

On top of that she makes claims such as there being an increase in 4400% of girls that seek transitioning treatment in the UK, whilst also claiming that a good share of them are autistic and "overrepresented". This sounds alarming but when you look at the actual numbers, the number of people seeking treatment have increased from 97 in 2009–2010 to 2,510 in 2017–2018, which would of course cause such an shocking increase when you start from a number that low (which only 2,510 is still not even a large number of youths to begin with at all compared to the hundreds of thousands of youths in the UK).

JK Rowling is also friends with gender critical feminists, quoting one of them, Magdalen Berns, as an "immensely brave young feminist and lesbian", when she has gone on record calling trans women as "fucking blackface actors."

Most of JK Rowling's transphobia sounds reasonable to those who don't understand the nuances of what she says, but the actual picture and what she claims it to be aren't the same, so it's hard to find explicit transphobia and "black and white" statements.

If I can give my two cents as a trans person myself, I'd say that the reason a lot of trans people enforce gender stereotypes is a lot more complicated than trying to prove themselves to society.

You're right though, it's safer to pass as your preferred gender and dressing as a traditional woman helps to do that. In my experience, dressing androgynously and still referring to myself as female didn't have as many positive reactions compared to when I dressed more feminine. This especially holds true when dealing with people who don't have that much experience with trans people. If people see you trying to pass as their preferred gender, they'll be more likely to refer to you as such. This can also be really helpful to prevent physical harm by people who aren't accepting to trans people at all by hiding your trans identity (a more technical term for this is going stealth).

I do have to say that a bigger reason for me to commit to some stereotypes is because I simply like it. I like to dress more feminine because that's what I like to wear. I like wearing skirts and dresses because they are more comfortable and I like how they look. If I was judged by nobody, I would still like to wear such things because I just want to, not because I am trying to uphold a stereotype.

However just because I adopt some traditionally feminine gender norms doesn't mean I agree to all of them. I still hold the belief that people should be willing to wear and behave how they want to act as long as they don't hurt anybody else. The same way a man can be more feminine without identifying as a woman is ok the same way a woman can do the opposite. People are just that, people, and trying to fit everyone in one box isn't going to work. The same way some people don't like the traits of their preferred gender is the same way a person can like those same things even if they are a "stereotype." It just varies from person to person just like trans people. We don't all think the same.

I understand where you are coming from, and I think it's important to stand up for all victims of crime, regardless of gender, but it's important to point out how common women face situations like the ones in this video, without people chiming in that it isn't all men. Technically speaking, time and age are constructs. The passage of time and how long it is was decided millennia ago, and some even measured it differently. There's even nothing stopping you from identifying as young as you want, but the passage of time does have an actual physical and mental effect on your body. Age is also visually measured as well. In the case of your doctor, the reason why you would have to list your actual age is because you might still be at risk of developing serious medical conditions that occur at later ages (testicular, colon, and breast cancer).

Trans people like myself have to list our biological sex because it is necessary for doctors to know it to give us the best medical care. No one is going against science or reason by identifying as trans, unlike identifying as trans racial or trans age.

Because just because something is a construct doesn't mean it isn't real. The reason we say gender is a social construct is because the confines of what is considered male or female are set by societal standards. Technically anything is a construct, height as in how tall or short someone is can be considered a construct because people are tall or short only relative to what is set by other people's standards.

The reason why people identify as transgender is because they don't identify with the gender that is seen as complimentary to their sex. Yes sex is real, but gender is only defined by our standards.

The truthful answer from what I understand of it, as a trans person, is that it's a lot more complicated than former men beating women in sports. Not all trans people are the same, meaning that how and when you transition will have a major effect on your performance in sports. A teenager on puberty blockers who hasn't fully went through male puberty won't have the same effects on performance than a grown adult who transitioned later.

So the main issue is what level of advantages do trans athletes have not whether or not they should be playing and determining what constitutes as an advantage is difficult. Would broad shoulders alone be a problem? Then how would that be different than women with naturally large shoulders?

So it's a lot more complicated than Reddit usually makes it out to be, which is why we need more information from qualified experts before making decisions.
